extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners / Office personnel (and patent practitioners evaluating obviousness)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing obviousness rejections based on an 'obvious to try' rationale under 35 U.S.C. §103, with emphasis on chemical/biotech examples but applicable across technologies. Explains factual findings and legal standards examiners should make (predictability, finite options, reasonable expectation of success, teaching away, common sense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite number of identified, predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR: when there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options within his or her technical grasp; in such circumstances the fact that a combination was obvious to try might show that it was obvious under §103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a central prerequisite for using an 'obvious to try' rationale to support obviousness. Examples where a finite set supported obviousness include Pfizer (53 pharmaceutically acceptable salts) and Perfect Web (three known potential solutions). Contrast cases (Takeda, Ortho-McNeil) where the solutions were not finite/small or were not predictable. Examiners must assess whether the prior art limits the solution space to a finite, identifiable, and predictable set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success / predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: An obvious-to-try conclusion is appropriate only when persons of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation that at least one of the identified options would be successful; predictability of results is emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the field was predictable and whether routine application of known techniques would likely achieve the claimed invention. Cases finding reasonable expectation of success include Alza (sustained release formulations) and Kubin (routine sequencing/isolating methods), while Sanofi and Ortho-McNeil illustrate that unpredictability or serendipity can defeat an obvious-to-try rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual inquiry into science/technology characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The obvious-to-try inquiry must be undertaken in the context of the subject matter, including the characteristics of the science or technology, its state of advance, the nature of the known choices, the specificity or generality of the prior art, and the predictability of results in the area of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze technical field specifics (e.g., chemical vs. mechanical unpredictability), how advanced the technology was, and whether prior art provided specific direction or only general suggestions. Abbott Labs v. Sandoz (quoted) highlights that these contextual factors are essential to the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try inappropriate when parameters must be varied without indication of critical ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Obvious-to-try is improperly equated with obviousness where one would have to vary all parameters or try numerous possible choices with no indication of which parameters are critical or which options are likely to succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the two Kubin/O'Farrell classes of improper obvious-to-try reasoning. If prior art gives no guidance as to which parameters matter, then trying many permutations does not support an obviousness conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try inappropriate when prior art gives only general guidance to explore a promising field
rubrics_metrics.description: Obvious-to-try is improper where the obvious step would be to explore a new technology or general approach and the prior art provides only broad guidance without specific direction to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the second Kubin/O'Farrell class. If prior art merely suggests exploring an area (but not specific, predictable avenues), that exploratory work is not sufficient to show obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Finite’ means small or easily traversed in context of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Federal Circuit precedent, 'finite' in KSR means 'small or easily traversed' relative to the field in question; a large universe of possible alternatives (even if theoretically finite) may not satisfy KSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ortho-McNeil emphasizes that the number of options must be tractable in context. A list of hundreds of millions of possible compounds will not make a claim obvious merely because it is finite; assess size relative to the art and practical traversability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a reason to select a particular lead compound or starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a reason in the prior art to select a particular starting compound or lead for modification; absent such reason—or where the prior art teaches away—an obviousness rejection is inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Takeda and Ortho-McNeil show that if the closest prior art had disadvantages that would deter selection as a lead, or if no teaching pointed to that lead, then an obvious-to-try rejection is improper. Examiners should look for art-based reasons supporting selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results or surprising properties defeat obvious-to-try
rubrics_metrics.description: When consideration of all evidence shows the outcome would not have been reasonably predictable and the inventor lacked a reasonable expectation of success, an obvious-to-try rationale is not appropriate; unexpected therapeutic advantages or surprising results can overcome a prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanofi (absolute stereoselectivity of D-isomer) and Bayer (bioavailability outcomes) illustrate that unexpected, non-predictable outcomes rebut obviousness. Examiners must consider post-filed evidence of unexpected properties where probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art that narrows the option set controls the analysis (consider reduced set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where prior art teachings funnel a formulator/worker toward a narrower set of options, that reduced set—not the larger theoretical universe—should be considered for an obvious-to-try inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bayer teaches that even if many possibilities exist in principle, specific prior art may guide the skilled artisan to a small subset of realistic options (e.g., two viable formulations); examiners should analyze the narrowed choice set when applying KSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining known references with routine methods can render claims obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art reference identifies an entity (e.g., a polypeptide) and routine, conventional methods would have been used to obtain the claimed invention (e.g., sequence and isolate nucleic acid), then a rejection may be proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kubin illustrates that the presence of conventional techniques (Sambrook) combined with a disclosure of the target molecule in the prior art supported an obviousness finding. Examiners should document the routine nature of methods and the reasonable expectation of success when relying on such combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invocation of common sense requires reasoned explanation and evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense may inform an obviousness analysis, but its use must be accompanied by a reasoned explanation that avoids conclusory generalizations and, where basic knowledge is not apparent on the record, require a factual foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect Web and precedents (In re Bozek, In re Zurko, DyStar, In re Kahn, B/E Aerospace) teach that examiners can rely on common sense only when they provide a reasoned analysis and evidentiary support; merely asserting common sense without record support is improper. See also cases noting limits (Arendi).

rubrics_metrics.name: No suggestion in prior art that a particular modification would address the problem -> not an obvious option
rubrics_metrics.description: If nothing in the prior art would have suggested the claimed change as an option to address the recognized problem, then the claimed solution would not have 'presented itself' as an obvious-to-try option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolls-Royce shows that absent any prior-art suggestion that, e.g., changing a sweep angle would solve endwall shock, that change would not have presented itself as an obvious option. Examiners should identify documentary or technical suggestion in the prior art before treating a modification as an available option.
